sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: Craterellus cinereus (ashen chanterelle) forms a small dark gray to black fruiting body with a cap distinct from the stem. The cap is usually about 1–4 cm across, though some European guides report up to 6 cm; it begins depressed, becomes funnel-shaped, and may develop a central perforation. Its margin is wavy to lobed. The pale gray to bluish-gray underside bears thick, blunt, branched ridges, sometimes cross-connected; they run down the stem and are not thin, separable blades. The dark gray to blackish stem is distinct, usually a few centimetres tall, sometimes grooved and tapering toward the base. Flesh is thin and grayish to blackish; its odor is described as sweet and fruity, sometimes reminiscent of plum.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This mycorrhizal species grows on soil among leaf litter, especially with beech and other broadleaf trees, often in groups or clusters. European guides report it in summer and autumn; timing varies with local climate. It has also been reported under conifers, but its association with broadleaf trees is better documented. Chestnut woods and calcareous soils occur in some habitat descriptions, but are not universal requirements.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Craterellus cornucopioides (horn of plenty / black trumpet) can grow in the same habitat. It is generally more uniformly trumpet-shaped, with a less clearly defined stem and a smooth or nearly smooth underside; C. cinereus has a more distinct stem and clearly visible gray ridges. Faerberia carbonaria can also be dark and funnel-shaped, but has thinner, paler gills and grows on burnt ground. Color alone is not enough to distinguish them: check the underside, stem, and habitat, and have any collection confirmed by a qualified person.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: The DGfM includes C. cinereus on its positive list of edible mushrooms; VAPKO classifies it B2, meaning permitted for commercial sale only under its list. These classifications do not confirm the identity or safety of any specimen; lookalikes remain possible and local harvesting rules may apply. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this entry or an image. If ingestion is uncertain or symptoms develop, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly and keep specimens or meal leftovers.

traits: Cap usually about 1–4 cm across, sometimes up to 6 cm; dark gray to black, depressed then funnel-shaped, with a wavy margin
Pale gray to bluish-gray underside with thick, blunt, branched and sometimes cross-connected ridges that run down the stem
Dark gray to blackish stem distinct from the cap, a few centimetres tall, sometimes grooved and tapering toward the base
Thin grayish to blackish flesh; odor described as sweet and fruity, sometimes reminiscent of plum
On soil and leaf litter in woods, especially with beech and other broadleaf trees; often clustered, in summer and autumn
safetyNote: The DGfM includes Craterellus cinereus on its positive list of edible mushrooms; VAPKO classifies it B2, permitted for commercial sale only under its list. These classifications do not confirm a wild specimen's identity. C. cornucopioides and Faerberia carbonaria can look similar. Seek a qualified confirmation and follow local rules. If ingestion is uncertain or symptoms develop, contact a poison centre or doctor promptly.
